segments.text: >> Hi everyone, and welcome to this Business Central Launch Edition session on BC Bench. My name is Joost. I'm the product owner for BC Bench, and today I'm here with my colleague. I'm Horan, software engineer on the BC Bench project.

Yep. As more and more development in Business Central AL is done by agents or assisted by agents, there's a need to to find out which model which MCP servers, which instructions, and which agent harness, as well as the tooling and skills given to these agents is the best combination to get the best results in your coding projects.

To find out which combination is the best, we've developed a benchmarking tool that lets us test all these combinations as an agent solves coding problems in Business Central. For this, we're introducing BC Bench.

This is a reproducible evaluation framework for AI coding agents working on real-world AL development tasks inspired by SweetBench. So, by using BC Bench, we can measure the performance of different AI models on real AI issues from our own backlog,

quantify the impact of any changes we make. So, if we're changing the MCP server or changing the LLM model used by the agents, we'll be able to measure if if that change leads to an improvement in results or or a degradation in results.

On top of that, as we're, you know, making progress with with new models and new MCP servers and new instructions, we're also able to track our progress towards 100% performance of these agents, meaning it gets all the problems right.

And then, finally, we can use the BC Bench to rapidly iterate on agent configurations. So, we can experiment with different setups and quickly find out if they're better or worse than what we tried before.
BC Bench is inspired by SweetBench in that it takes real-world boxes and benchmarks as it tries to fix these boxes. SweetBench is widely used by the AI research community.
It's widely recognized as the benchmarking tool to see how good different LLM models and agent harnesses are at solving coding problems. And over the last year or so, it has demonstrated measurably

that models have improved in solving these coding problems. Now, with BC Bench, we've adapted this idea to AL and Business Central. So, we can figure out how good these models are at fixing bugs in Business Central specifically.

So, why does Business Central need its own benchmark next to SweetBench? The reality here is that general coding benchmarks like SweetBench do not reflect the realities that a Business Central developer faces every day.

Business Central has a smaller ecosystem than other coding languages, and there's a lot of domain-specific tooling and knowledge that only applies to Business Central and wouldn't be reflected in the benchmarking results you would get from a tool like SweetBench.

This is demonstrated by just the size of open-source GitHub repositories. You can see that in Python, there are more than 2 million repositories that are open-source that a benchmark can take issues from, can take results from, and ultimately learn from.
Whereas in AL, we only have 330 as of the time of this recording. So, the the data set here with the the AL ecosystem and the domain-specific knowledge is simply a lot smaller and more specific.

So, how does BC Bench work when it comes to to bug fixing? In our normal development flow that we've had for years, and we have a long history of within the Business Central team, we have many bug reports that a human BC developer would take up and then deliver a fix for.

This fix consists of a functional fix as well as a unit test to make sure that this issue is actually fixed in future developments as well. Now, what we do to develop BC Bench is we take these same bug reports,

now have these bug reports given the same inputs as the human BC developer would have had, to the coding agent and have the coding agent generate a fix. Then, the coding agent also verifies that fix using the unit test that has previously been developed by the BC developer.

And using that unit test, we can now see whether the results that the coding agent delivered passed or failed. The data set is is quite simple. So, we've taken real Business Central bugs from our own backlog that we've collected over the years,

and we've put them or we've collected them into um into the benchmarking data set. So, you can see the description of the of the bug in this case, the title, the repo steps are going into the problem statements for the agent.

The unit test that was developed by the by the developer when this bug was fixed is also included in the benchmark BC Bench data set so that the agent can see what test needs to pass to evaluate whether it has a successful result as it runs the benchmark.
